newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels close in on Zaire's third city.
newsitem.headline: Rebels close in on Zaire's third city.

text.p: Rebels are closing in on Zaire's third city of Kisangani where the army has sown land mines and deployed mercenaries to try to halt their advance, regional and local military sources say.

The government on Monday denied rebel claims to have surrounded Kisangani, the headquarters of army operations against the revolt in the east which began in October and has been steadily spreading west since then.

One regional military analyst and local military sources said Tutsi-led rebels were massing on the southeastern flank and advancing from the north but the analyst predicted they might opt to stop and consolidate if they met stiff opposition.
"The momentum is certainly with the rebels. But they may be forced to stop and consolidate their positions around the city if they meet stiff resistance," he told Reuters.

Government and rebels have attached huge symbolic value to Kisangani. It is strategically placed on the Zaire River, which flows down to the capital Kinshasa. Witnesses say troops have begun stopping and checking all boats heading west.
The Zairean defence ministry says rebels are within 100 km (60 miles) to the north and northeast of the city and within 50 km (30 miles) to the southeast.

Independent sources place the rebels closer in the north, where they report that, using the Lindi River, the rebels were able to take the town of Bengamisa last week and move within 40 km (25 miles) of Kisangani.
Regional military analysts say that should Kisangani fall copper-rich Shaba province in the south, and diamond-rich Kasai could follow in a domino effect.

In Geneva, the European Union humanitarian affairs commissioner Emma Bonino accused the Tutsi-led rebels of hunting down Hutu refugees "like wild game" and killing them in retaliation for the 1994 genocide of Tutsis in Rwanda.
She accused the international community of "cowardice, a lot of lies and an enormous dose of cynicism" in its handling of the refugee crisis spawned by the revolt.
Hutu refugees have been flooding into Ubundu, 100 km (60 miles) south of Kisangani. The U.N. World Food Programme said the sudden influx overwhelmed the four aid workers there.
"Tens of thousands of refugees poured into Ubundu over the weekend and there are possibly as many as 100,000 there now," said spokeswoman Michele Quintaglie.
An estimated 170,000 refugees fled Tingi Tingi to the south east last month before it fell to rebels. Quintaglie said the refugees were frightened and talking about leaving Ubundu.

The refugees include Hutus from Rwanda and Burundi. Those from Rwanda fled in 1994 fearing repisals after Tutsi-dominated exiles fought their way home and toppled Hutu hardliners widely blamed for the genocide.
Hutu hardliners have been fighting alongside Zaire's army. Critics accuse them of forcing refugees to retreat with them.

The rebels say they want to topple Mobutu Sese Seko, Zaire's leader of over three decades. Mobutu had cancer surgery in Europe in August and has been out of the country for most of the time since then. He has been in France since last month.
